That's not how modern AI works. It's not like there's a whole bunch of conditions, "if this and this and this then do that.. else if this and this then do that.." on for millions of lines. Nearly all AIs seeing rapid evolution today are using various forms of deep learning. With a deep learning AI you don't directly program the AI's behavior but instead program the means to help the AI develop its own behavior in response to stimuli.

It's like the recent Go AI. The developers of that AI were far from world class players and certainly couldn't tell you exactly what the AI would do in any situation - they were certainly in no position to teach anybody how to play! What they did instead was developed software capable of teaching itself and learning from experience which is absolutely necessary as Go is a very strategic game that is absolutely impossible to even begin to brute force. The AI went 5-1 against the world's strongest human player. Before this AI, no software had ever beaten a top ranked human in a fair (no odds) game of Go, let alone a match.

Martensite is not a class of steel but rather a state. Martensite is used to describe how the carbon atoms are diffused into the steel crystal matrix.
High carbon is my personal favorite. No corrosion resistance so you have to keep it oiled and take care of it. Unlike the stainless varieties.

The down side is the steel doesn't retain is sharpness as well as the super steels, how ever unlike the super steels, a couple of passes of 1095 over a stone and your edge is back up to snuff. 1095 is the easiest sharpening steel there is.

High carbon cold tempered steel is very nice. It is so brittle that is is very sharp and can be made very sharp compared to some of the harder more durable stainless steels. High carbon cold tempered steel is underrated and maybe considered cheap and crappy but if you want an ultra sharp knive that's easy to sharpen it's great. I don't make knives personally but used to collect them and these are my two favourites.
